top_level_objectives: Explain the fundamental principle of VSEPR theory and how electrostatic repulsion dictates molecular shape.
Differentiate between electron-domain geometry and molecular geometry.
Identify the five core electron-domain geometries based on coordination number.
Predict the effects of non-bonding lone pairs on molecular bond angles and shape symmetry.
Determine the correct thermodynamic placement of lone pairs in trigonal bipyramidal and octahedral structures.

scenes.brief_purpose: Visualize and feel electrostatic repulsion by dragging electron domains around a central atom to see how they automatically push apart to maximize spatial distance.
key_visuals: A floating 3D central atom in AR with 2 to 4 glowing green 'electron domain' lobes attached.
Dynamic, glowing force vectors (arrows) showing repulsion strength between domains in real time.
An 'Energy State' bar that transitions from red (unstable, high repulsion) to green (stable, lowest repulsion).
student_actions: Grab and drag one of the electron domains close to another domain using hands or controllers, feeling haptic resistance.
Release the domain and observe the domains spring back and settle into an optimal, symmetrical arrangement (e.g., linear or tetrahedral).
Toggle the visibility of force vectors and electrostatic repulsion fields.

scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce the five fundamental electron-domain geometries (linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, octahedral) before introducing lone pairs.
key_visuals: Five rotating 3D generic AB_x structures arranged on a virtual lab bench.
Hovering labels indicating idealized bond angles (180, 120, 109.5, 90/120, 90 degrees).
A floating dashboard listing the names of the five core electron-domain geometries.
student_actions: Pick up and rotate each of the five core shapes to inspect them from all angles.
Drag and drop the correct geometry name card to its corresponding 3D shape.
Press a 'Show Angles' button to project 3D angle indicators directly inside the structures.

scenes.scene_name: Lone Pairs and Bond Angle Compression
scenes.brief_purpose: Contrast electron-domain geometry with molecular geometry, showing how non-bonding lone pairs compress bond angles in the tetrahedral family (CH4, NH3, H2O).
key_visuals: Side-by-side comparison of Methane, Ammonia, and Water molecules in 3D.
Translucent, bulbous purple lobes representing non-bonding lone pairs, which physically occupy more angular space than bonding pairs.
Dynamic angle arcs displaying 109.5 degrees for Methane, 107.3 degrees for Ammonia, and 104.5 degrees for Water.
student_actions: Interact with a slider to expand/contract the lone pair electron cloud size and watch the adjacent hydrogen bonds dynamically squeeze closer together.
Toggle between displaying the 'Electron-Domain Geometry' (all three are tetrahedral) and the 'Molecular Geometry' (tetrahedral, trigonal pyramidal, and bent).

scenes.scene_name: Spatial Decisions in Trigonal Bipyramidal Systems
scenes.brief_purpose: Demonstrate why lone pairs preferentially occupy equatorial positions rather than axial positions in five-domain systems to minimize 90-degree repulsions.
key_visuals: A large 3D model of a trigonal bipyramidal coordinate system, highlighting the axial (90 degree) and equatorial (120 degree) spatial relationships.
Two side-by-side comparative models of SF4: one with the lone pair placed axially, and one with the lone pair placed equatorially.
A glowing 'Repulsion Meter' indicating the high-energy instability of the axial lone-pair configuration.
student_actions: Manually slot a virtual lone pair (purple lobe) into either the axial or equatorial position of a sulfur tetrafluoride (SF4) template.
Observe the real-time 'Repulsion Energy' readout spike in red for the incorrect axial placement and drop to green for the correct equatorial (seesaw) placement.
Rotate the final stable seesaw geometry of SF4 to observe its asymmetry.

scenes.brief_purpose: Explore high-coordination 6-domain systems (SF6, BrF5, XeF4) and observe how multiple lone pairs position themselves 180 degrees apart to minimize mutual repulsion.
key_visuals: 3D molecular models of Sulfur Hexafluoride (octahedral), Bromine Pentafluoride (square pyramidal), and Xenon Tetrafluoride (square planar).
For XeF4, two prominent purple lone-pair lobes positioned directly opposite one another along the z-axis.
A flat grid visualizer highlighting the perfectly co-planar arrangement of the four fluorine atoms around Xenon.
student_actions: Rotate the Xenon Tetrafluoride (XeF4) molecule to verify that the four fluorine atoms lie in a single, flat 2D plane.
Tap on the lone pairs to toggle them off and see how the remaining atoms form a 'square planar' molecular geometry.
Measure the F-Xe-F angles to confirm they remain at exactly 90 degrees due to the symmetrical cancellation of the lone-pair repulsions.

scenes.brief_purpose: Apply VSEPR rules to identify, construct, and name the geometry of an unknown chemical formula starting from its Lewis structure.
key_visuals: A virtual clipboard showing a 2D Lewis structure (e.g., SO2 or I3-).
An interactive workbench with a central atom and a bin containing bonding pairs (single/double bonds) and lone pairs.
A multiple-choice evaluation portal for selecting electron-domain geometry and molecular geometry names.
student_actions: Construct the 3D molecule by snapping the correct number of bonds and lone pairs from the bin onto the central atom.
Press the 'Apply VSEPR Physics' button to trigger the electrostatic simulation and watch the constructed molecule relax into its stable shape.
Select the correct electron-domain geometry and molecular geometry names from the virtual evaluation portal to complete the lab.
